title: AI Unlocked: Medicine
blurb: For medical students, physicians, and clinical teams: safe clinical prompting, documentation scribes, decision-support and research tools compared head-to-head, imaging frontiers, and a mentor-reviewed clinical AI workflow. 8 in-depth modules, 80 board-style MCQs, printable certificate.

modules.d: The evidence, the economics, and the honest limits of AI in medicine.
modules.body:
Why this course exists

Medicine is in a documented crisis of time. Studies across health systems consistently find physicians spending roughly two hours on the electronic health record and desk work for every one hour of direct patient care, with "pajama time" — after-hours charting — a leading driver of burnout. Meanwhile the biomedical literature doubles at a pace no human can read: PubMed indexes well over a million new citations per year. Into this gap arrives a technology that is genuinely good at exactly the tasks consuming clinicians: transcribing, summarizing, drafting, retrieving, and translating. The clinicians who thrive in the next decade will not be replaced by AI — they will be the ones who direct it with skill and skepticism. This course builds that skill and that skepticism in equal measure.

Cardiologist Eric Topol argues in Deep Medicine that AI’s greatest gift to medicine may be restoring its human side — returning time and presence to the clinician-patient bond. The WHO agrees on the condition: its guidance holds that AI offers "great promise" for health only where ethics and human oversight govern design. That double conviction — leverage plus guardrails — runs through all eight modules.

A working taxonomy: four kinds of medical AI

Confusion about "AI in medicine" usually comes from lumping four very different things together. Keep them separate and every headline becomes easier to judge:

  • 1. Generative assistants (LLMs): ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and their medical derivatives. They generate text: notes, letters, explanations, differentials-as-text. They are trained on the human record, not connected to truth — brilliance and hallucination come from the same mechanism.
  • 2. Ambient documentation (scribes): systems that listen to the visit with consent and draft the clinical note. Narrow, mature, and already deployed at scale across major health systems.
  • 3. Regulated diagnostic devices: FDA-cleared (and internationally approved) algorithms in imaging, cardiology, ophthalmology, pathology. These are medical devices with defined intended uses, validation studies, and failure modes — closer to a CT scanner than to a chatbot.
  • 4. Predictive/operational models: sepsis early-warning scores, no-show predictors, bed-management forecasts. Live inside health systems, largely invisible to patients, and the source of most cautionary tales about bias and drift.

What the evidence actually shows (state of play)

  • Documentation: peer-reviewed evaluations and large health-system deployments of ambient scribes report meaningful reductions in after-hours charting and burnout scores, with note quality rated equal or better after clinician editing. This is the most robust value case in clinical AI today.
  • Knowledge questions: frontier LLMs now pass USMLE-style examinations comfortably and, in blinded studies, their written answers to patient questions have been rated as more complete and — uncomfortably — more empathetic than rushed human replies. Passing an exam is not practicing medicine; it is, however, a real capability signal.
  • Imaging: in screening mammography, large prospective European studies have shown AI-supported reading can maintain or improve cancer detection while cutting radiologist workload substantially. Diabetic retinopathy screening systems operate autonomously at the point of care under regulatory clearance.
  • Cautionary record: a landmark analysis of a widely used commercial risk algorithm found it systematically under-referred Black patients because it used healthcare cost as a proxy for healthcare need — a bias lesson every clinician should be able to recount. Similarly, a widely deployed proprietary sepsis model was found in external validation to miss a large fraction of sepsis cases while generating heavy alert burdens. External validation matters.

The honest limits — memorize these five

  • Hallucination: LLMs generate plausible falsehoods — fabricated citations, invented drug doses, confident wrong facts — because they predict text rather than retrieve truth.
  • Training cutoff and drift: models don’t know last month’s guideline change unless connected to live sources.
  • Distribution shift: a model validated in Boston may fail in Bamenda — or in the hospital across town. Population, equipment, and coding practices all shift performance.
  • Automation bias: humans over-trust confident machines. The corrective is procedural (verification steps), not attitudinal (telling yourself you’ll be careful).
  • Accountability: no AI carries a medical license. Every output that touches a patient or a chart is professionally yours after you accept it.
Course rule (Team21 Commandment 2, clinical edition): AI drafts, the clinician decides. Nothing generated in this course reaches a patient or a chart without your professional review — and Module 8 makes that rule institutional.
Reading companion: Eric Topol, Deep Medicine (the humanist case); WHO, Ethics and Governance of AI for Health (the governance frame — six principles from protecting human autonomy to ensuring inclusiveness and equity). Skim both this week; they anchor the capstone.

quiz.q: A common finding across time-motion studies of physicians is approximately…
opts: Equal time on EHR and patients
Two hours of EHR/desk work per hour of direct patient care
quiz.x: The ~2:1 EHR-to-patient-time ratio is a consistent finding and explains why documentation is AI’s highest-value clinical target.

quiz.q: Which category of medical AI does an ambient scribe belong to?
quiz.x: Scribes draft notes from consented visit audio — narrow, mature, and distinct from diagnostic devices or chatbots.

quiz.q: LLM hallucination is best described as…
opts: A software bug vendors will patch soon
Plausible falsehoods arising from the same predictive mechanism as correct output
A rare event affecting only old models
quiz.x: Prediction over text produces both brilliance and fabrication; it is intrinsic, so verification must be procedural.

quiz.q: The landmark algorithmic-bias study found a commercial risk tool under-served Black patients because it used…
opts: Healthcare cost as a proxy for healthcare need
quiz.x: Cost proxied need; unequal access meant equally sick Black patients generated lower costs and thus lower risk scores.

quiz.q: External validation of a widely deployed proprietary sepsis model showed…
opts: Missed cases and heavy alert burden outside the development setting
Regulators had cleared it as a device
quiz.x: Distribution shift and weak external validity are recurring lessons of predictive models in practice.

quiz.q: AI passing USMLE-style exams primarily demonstrates…
opts: A capability signal on medical knowledge questions, not clinical competence
quiz.x: Exam performance signals knowledge capability; practice involves examination, uncertainty, procedures, and accountability.

quiz.q: In screening mammography, large prospective studies of AI support have shown…
opts: Higher detection with reduced radiologist workload is achievable
quiz.x: Prospective European trials showed maintained-or-improved detection with major workload reduction — assistive, not replacement.

quiz.q: Automation bias is corrected best by…
quiz.x: Humans reliably over-trust confident machines; the fix is designed-in checks, not intentions.

quiz.q: The WHO’s AI-for-health guidance conditions AI’s promise on…
opts: Ethics, equity, and human oversight in design and use
quiz.x: WHO’s six principles — autonomy, safety, transparency, accountability, equity, sustainability — are the field’s governance constitution.

quiz.q: Who bears professional responsibility for an AI-drafted note you sign?
quiz.x: Acceptance transfers full professional ownership — the foundation of the ‘AI drafts, clinician decides’ rule.

modules.d: Data discipline, the CLEAR framework at clinical grade, and the prompt patterns that survive contact with real practice.
modules.body:
Patient privacy before prompting — the non-negotiable layer

Under HIPAA (US) and equivalent regimes (GDPR in Europe, and national health-data laws elsewhere), Protected Health Information includes far more than names: dates of birth, medical record numbers, facial images, device identifiers, and — the trap most clinicians miss — combinations that re-identify, such as a rare diagnosis plus a small town plus an age. Consumer chatbots are not covered entities and offer no Business Associate Agreement (BAA); pasting PHI into them can constitute a reportable breach regardless of how helpful the output was.

  • Green path: institution-approved tools operating under a BAA or equivalent contract (many health systems now deploy HIPAA-eligible instances of major models), with data-retention and training-use terms in writing.
  • Amber path: consumer tools with rigorous de-identification — remove all 18 HIPAA identifier categories AND ask the re-identification question: could a motivated reader in my community identify this patient? If unsure, don’t.
  • Red path: raw clinical text, images with faces or identifiers, or protection-sensitive cases in any unapproved tool. Never.

De-identification in practice (do this, not just know it)

  • Swap specifics for clinical equivalents: "67-year-old man" not the name and DOB; "a regional referral hospital" not yours; "day 3 of admission" not the date.
  • Shift or bucket ages over 89, exact dates, and rare-disease geography.
  • Strip metadata from images; crop identifiers; never upload a face without explicit, documented consent and an approved tool.

CLEAR at clinical grade

The Team21 CLEAR framework (Persona · Tone · Format · Details · Target audience, plus Context, Reference, Iterate, Evaluate) becomes far more powerful when the Reference element carries clinical standards:

  • Persona: "You are a board-certified internist and medical educator who cites guidelines and flags uncertainty explicitly."
  • Format: name the artifact — SOAP note, SBAR handoff, ISBAR referral, discharge summary, AVS at 6th-grade reading level, table of differentials with discriminators.
  • Reference: "Guideline-concordant (name the guideline body relevant to you); distinguish what you know from what you infer; list every claim I must verify."
  • Evaluate: end prompts with "State your three largest uncertainties" — models are startlingly good at self-flagging when asked, and silent when not.

Seven prompt patterns that earn their place in your practice

  • The structured note: "Convert this de-identified encounter narrative into a SOAP note. Mark [INFERRED] anything not explicitly stated." The inference-marking instruction is the safety feature.
  • The dual-ranked differential: "Rank by likelihood AND separately by danger; for each, one discriminating question, one exam finding, one initial test." Dual ranking mirrors real clinical reasoning — common things commonly, deadly things always.
  • The devil’s-advocate consult: "My working diagnosis is X. Argue for the two most dangerous alternatives I might be anchoring away from." Anti-anchoring as a service.
  • The literacy transformer: "Rewrite these discharge instructions at 6th-grade level; keep all red-flag warnings verbatim in bold; then produce a French version." Health-literacy studies show most patient materials are written years above average reading level — this closes a real safety gap.
  • The guideline delta: "Summarize what changed between the prior and current guideline on [topic], as a table: recommendation, old, new, strength of evidence." (Then verify against the guideline itself — this pattern accelerates verification, never replaces it.)
  • The teach-back generator: "Write 5 teach-back questions to confirm this patient understood their new anticoagulant."
  • The attending simulator: "Act as a skeptical attending; pimp me on the physiology behind this presentation, one question at a time, escalating difficulty; correct me bluntly."

Verification discipline — the 60-second rule

For any clinical fact you did not already know: verify in a primary source before use. Doses and interactions against a formulary; claims against the guideline or a Module 4 evidence tool; citations by opening them (AI-fabricated references are the signature failure — assume fabricated until the DOI resolves). Sixty seconds of verification is the price of the hours AI saves you; clinicians who skip it eventually make the newspapers.

🧪 Interactive Lab — run this now

You are a board-certified clinician-educator. I will paste a DE-IDENTIFIED case. Produce: (1) a SOAP note marking every inference [INFERRED]; (2) a differential ranked by likelihood AND by danger with one discriminator each; (3) discharge instructions at 6th-grade reading level with red-flags in bold; (4) the same instructions in French; (5) a list titled VERIFY BEFORE USE containing every dose, claim, and citation I must confirm, with where to confirm each. Case: [paste de-identified case].

plAIbox™: run the lab on one real (de-identified) case from your week. Keep an error log: every correction you made to the AI output, categorized (factual / inferential / tone / omission). That log is a required capstone artifact — and the fastest calibration tool you will ever use.

quiz.q: Which is PHI even without a name attached?
opts: A rare diagnosis + small town + exact age combination
quiz.x: Re-identifying combinations are PHI; the 18 identifiers include dates, locations smaller than state, and any unique combination.

quiz.q: A Business Associate Agreement (BAA) matters because…
opts: It contractually binds the tool vendor to health-data protections
It is required for open-source models only
quiz.x: Covered entities may share PHI only with vendors under BAA-equivalent protections; consumer chatbots offer none.

quiz.q: Pasting an identifiable patient story into a consumer chatbot is best classified as…
opts: Fine if the output is deleted
quiz.x: Breach status depends on disclosure, not on how useful the output was or whether you delete the chat.

quiz.q: The [INFERRED] marking instruction in note prompts exists to…
opts: Expose what the model assumed beyond the source text
quiz.x: LLMs fluently fill gaps; forcing inference-marking turns silent assumptions into visible, checkable ones.

quiz.q: Dual-ranking a differential (likelihood AND danger) mirrors which clinical principle?
opts: Common things commonly, deadly things always
quiz.x: Separate danger ranking keeps can’t-miss diagnoses in view even when improbable.

quiz.q: Most patient education materials fail because they are written…
opts: Years above average patient reading level
quiz.x: Health-literacy research consistently shows materials outpacing reading levels; the literacy transformer pattern targets this directly.

quiz.q: The correct default posture toward an AI-provided citation is…
opts: Assume fabricated until you open and confirm it
Ask the model to confirm it
quiz.x: Fabricated references are the signature LLM failure; a well-formatted fake looks identical to a real one.

quiz.q: Ending clinical prompts with ‘state your three largest uncertainties’ exploits the fact that models…
opts: Self-flag well when asked and stay silent when not
quiz.x: Uncertainty elicitation is cheap and materially improves the safety profile of outputs.

quiz.q: Which case is safest for a consumer tool after de-identification?
opts: A routine presentation with all 18 identifier categories removed and no re-identifying combination
A face photo with cropped name
quiz.x: Protection-sensitive and public-figure cases stay off consumer tools regardless; faces are biometric identifiers.

quiz.q: The 60-second rule states…
opts: Any clinical fact you didn’t already know gets primary-source verification before use
AI answers expire in a minute
quiz.x: Fixed verification habits, not vigilance intentions, are what prevent AI-accelerated errors.

modules.t: Tool Study I: Documentation & Ambient Scribes
modules.d: The market mapped, the economics computed, and the pilot playbook for getting one.
modules.body:
Why scribes are the beachhead

Documentation is where clinical AI pays for itself first because the task is bounded (one visit → one note), the ground truth is nearby (you were in the room), and the value is immediate (your evening back). Health systems deploying ambient scribes at scale report the largest burnout-score improvements of any recent intervention. Master this category and you will understand how to evaluate every other one.

How ambient scribes actually work

  • Capture: with explicit patient consent, the visit audio is recorded (phone or room mic). Consent scripts and jurisdictional recording laws are part of deployment, not afterthoughts.
  • ASR + diarization: speech-to-text with speaker separation — robust to accents and interruptions in modern systems, still challenged by heavy crosstalk and some code-switching.
  • Generation: an LLM transforms transcript to note in your template (SOAP, APSO, specialty formats), often with orders, problem lists, and patient instructions drafted alongside.
  • Review & sign: you edit and sign. Editing time is the honest metric — a scribe that saves dictation but demands heavy correction saves nothing.

The market, mapped by how you buy

  • Enterprise (bought by health systems): Microsoft DAX Copilot (Nuance) — the incumbent heavyweight, deep Epic integration, procured institutionally; Abridge — enterprise-grade with strong published evidence and major system partnerships, similarly institution-level. If you are employed by a large system, these arrive via your CMIO, not your credit card.
  • Self-serve (bought by clinicians): Heidi Health — free tier plus paid plans, minutes-to-start, popular with GPs, students, and clinics worldwide including low-resource settings; Freed — subscription (~$99/month class), built for independent clinicians, minimal IT; Suki — solo and group licensing with real EHR integrations (Epic, Cerner, athena), the mid-market bridge.
  • Watch the churn: this market moves quarterly — pricing, tiers, and EHR integrations in this module are teaching snapshots. Your capstone matrix requires you to verify current terms, which is itself the skill.

The selection matrix (your capstone artifact)

  • Integration: writes into your EHR vs copy-paste (copy-paste is fine solo, fails at clinic scale).
  • Consent & legality: recording-consent workflow matched to your jurisdiction (one-party vs all-party consent states/countries differ).
  • Template quality in YOUR specialty: a scribe brilliant in primary care may fumble psychiatry’s nuance or ophthalmology’s notation — trial with your own visit types.
  • Contract: BAA/DPA, data retention, training-use opt-out, breach terms — in writing.
  • Economics: price per clinician per month ÷ minutes saved per day. At even 30 minutes/day saved, a $99/month tool costs roughly $0.16 per saved minute — the cheapest clinician time ever purchased. Compute your own number honestly, including editing time.
  • Edge behavior: accents, interpreter visits, telehealth audio, offline/low-bandwidth conduct.

The pilot playbook (how individuals move institutions)

  • Week 0: pick 2 self-serve tools; get IT/privacy sign-off for a de-identified or consented trial per policy.
  • Weeks 1–2: 10 visits per tool. Log: minutes to complete note before vs after, edits per note, patient reactions to consent.
  • Week 3: one-page memo to your medical director — time data, quality samples, consent workflow, cost per clinician, and the ask (a funded 5-clinician pilot). Template provided in course resources. This memo has launched more institutional deployments than any vendor demo.
🧪 Interactive Lab

Act as a health-IT procurement analyst. Build me a scribe selection matrix as a table: rows = [tools I am considering]; columns = EHR integration, consent workflow fit for [my jurisdiction], specialty template quality for [my specialty], contract protections (BAA/DPA, training opt-out), monthly cost, estimated minutes saved per day, cost per saved minute, and open risks. Then draft the one-page pilot memo to my medical director using placeholder data I will replace.

quiz.q: The honest efficiency metric for a scribe is…
quiz.x: A scribe requiring heavy correction saves nothing; editing time is where value is proven or lost.

quiz.q: Enterprise scribes like DAX Copilot and Abridge typically reach clinicians via…
opts: Institutional procurement through the health system
quiz.x: They are bought by systems; individuals influence that via pilot data, not credit cards.

quiz.q: An independent clinician with no IT department should shortlist…
opts: Self-serve tools like Heidi, Freed, or Suki solo
quiz.x: Self-serve tools onboard in minutes and price per-clinician — the solo path.

quiz.q: Recording consent requirements…
opts: Vary by jurisdiction (one-party vs all-party) and must shape your workflow
quiz.x: Consent law differs across states and countries; deployment includes a compliant consent script.

quiz.q: At $99/month and 30 minutes saved daily (~20 clinic days), cost per saved minute is roughly…
quiz.x: $99 ÷ 600 minutes ≈ $0.165 — the economics clinicians should compute with their own honest numbers.

quiz.q: Diarization refers to…
opts: Separating and labeling speakers in the transcript
quiz.x: Speaker separation lets the system distinguish clinician, patient, and family in generation.

quiz.q: Why trial a scribe on YOUR visit types?
opts: Template quality varies sharply by specialty
quiz.x: Primary-care excellence doesn’t guarantee psychiatric nuance or procedural-note precision.

quiz.q: A training-use opt-out clause governs…
opts: Whether your patients’ data may train vendor models
quiz.x: Contract terms on secondary data use are a core selection criterion, not fine print.

quiz.q: The pilot playbook converts individual enthusiasm into institutional adoption chiefly through…
opts: A one-page memo with measured time data and a funded-pilot ask
quiz.x: Medical directors act on measured minutes and a concrete, small ask.

quiz.q: Pricing/integration details in this module should be treated as…
opts: Teaching snapshots you must re-verify — verification is the skill
quiz.x: The scribe market moves quarterly; your capstone matrix requires current terms.

modules.t: Tool Study II: Knowledge & Decision Support
modules.d: Matching the tool to the question: point-of-care evidence, differentials, and the research engine stack.
modules.body:
The taxonomy of clinical questions

Clinicians ask four distinguishable kinds of questions, and the tool that excels at one fails at another. Mislabeling the question is the root of most disappointment with clinical AI:

  • Background ("What is X?"): settled knowledge — mechanisms, classifications, definitions. General LLMs excel; risk is low because errors are checkable against any textbook.
  • Foreground ("In this patient, should I…?"): evidence-dependent decisions. This is where citation-grounded tools earn their existence.
  • Reasoning support ("What am I missing?"): differential expansion, anti-anchoring. LLMs are strong brainstorm partners here precisely because breadth beats precision at this step.
  • Synthesis ("What does the literature say?"): research-grade questions needing systematic retrieval — the Module 5 stack.

The point-of-care evidence tier

  • OpenEvidence: free for verified clinicians (registration/NPI-class verification); answers foreground questions with citations drawn from the literature; has spread through US residency programs at remarkable speed precisely because it closes the citation gap that makes bare LLMs unsafe for foreground use.
  • UpToDate (with arriving AI features): the editorial gold standard — humans synthesize, grade, and take responsibility; institutional or personal subscription. When stakes are high and time is short, curated beats generated.
  • Glass Health: AI-assisted differentials and plan drafting built for clinicians; subscription with trial; particularly strong as a teaching scaffold — compare its differential to yours and interrogate the gaps.
  • General LLMs (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini): unbeatable for background explanation, drafting, transformation, and reasoning support; for foreground facts, treat every claim as unverified until checked against the tier above. The same model that beautifully explains renal physiology will occasionally invent a dosing threshold with identical confidence.

The research engine stack (preview of Module 5)

  • Elicit: screen and extract from papers at scale — inclusion screening, structured data extraction into tables; free tier + paid.
  • Consensus: "what does the literature say about X" with citation-backed synthesis and study-level claims.
  • Scite: the killer feature — shows whether citing papers support or contrast a claim, turning citation counts into citation directions.
  • Semantic Scholar + PubMed: the free foundations under every stack; modern PubMed plus an LLM for query-building is still the workhorse of serious searching.

Failure modes by tool class (know these cold)

  • Bare LLMs on foreground questions: fabricated specifics — the classic. Mitigation: citation-grounded tools or verify-every-claim discipline.
  • Citation-grounded tools: real citations, sometimes shallow reading of them — the paper exists but says less than implied. Mitigation: open the key citation for consequential decisions.
  • Curated references: lag on brand-new evidence and cost money. Mitigation: pair with alert services for your specialty.
  • All tools: your question framing dominates output quality — garbage question, confident garbage answer. The four-type taxonomy IS the prompt-engineering.
🧪 Interactive Lab — the four-way bake-off

I am comparing clinical knowledge tools. Here is one real foreground question from my practice this week: [state it precisely, PICO-style if possible]. First, classify my question (background / foreground / reasoning / synthesis) and critique its framing. Then answer it as well as you can, explicitly separating: (a) what you are confident of, (b) what you infer, (c) exactly which claims I must verify and the best primary source for each. I will run this same question through a citation-grounded tool and compare.

plAIbox™ (graded): run one real foreground question through four routes — a general LLM, OpenEvidence (or equivalent), UpToDate if you have access, and manual PubMed. Build a one-page comparison: speed, citation quality, accuracy, and precisely where each route would have misled you. Present to your cohort; the collective error map is the real curriculum.

quiz.q: “In this diabetic patient with CKD, should I start drug X?” is which question type?
quiz.x: Patient-specific, evidence-dependent decisions are foreground questions — the citation-grounded tier’s home ground.

quiz.q: OpenEvidence’s core design advantage for clinicians is…
opts: It is a chatbot with personality
Citation-grounded answers to clinical questions, free for verified clinicians
quiz.x: Grounding answers in retrievable literature closes the fabrication gap that makes bare LLMs unsafe for foreground use.

quiz.q: UpToDate’s enduring value proposition versus generated answers is…
opts: Human editorial synthesis with graded recommendations and accountability
quiz.x: Curated, responsibility-bearing synthesis is a different product class from on-the-fly generation.

quiz.q: The strongest legitimate LLM use in the taxonomy is…
opts: Reasoning support: differential expansion and anti-anchoring
quiz.x: Breadth beats precision at the ‘what am I missing’ step, and errors there are caught downstream by workup.

quiz.q: Scite’s distinctive feature is showing…
opts: Whether citing papers support or contrast a claim
quiz.x: Citation direction (supporting vs contrasting) converts raw counts into evidential meaning.

quiz.q: ‘Real citation, shallow reading’ is the signature failure of…
quiz.x: The paper exists but supports less than implied — open key citations for consequential decisions.

quiz.q: Elicit’s core strength is…
opts: Screening and structured extraction across many papers
quiz.x: It industrializes the screening/extraction stages of review work.

quiz.q: For a brand-new trial published last week, the weakest source is likely…
quiz.x: Curated references trade freshness for reliability; pair them with alerts for your field.

quiz.q: The dominant determinant of output quality across ALL tools is…
opts: How precisely you frame the question
quiz.x: Question taxonomy and framing are the prompt engineering of clinical knowledge work.

quiz.q: A safe rule for bare-LLM foreground answers is…
opts: Every specific claim is unverified until checked against a grounded source
quiz.x: Confidence and correctness are uncorrelated at the specifics level; verification is non-optional.

modules.t: AI for Medical Research & Academic Writing
modules.d: From question to published paper: the accelerated pipeline, the statistics guardrails, and the integrity rules journals now enforce.
modules.body:
The research pipeline, accelerated stage by stage

  • 1. Question formulation: "Convert my vague interest — [topic] — into three answerable questions in PICO format (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome); for each, state the study design that could answer it and the datasets or populations that would be required." Ten minutes of this dialogue routinely saves a month of drift.
  • 2. Search strategy: LLMs draft Boolean strings with MeSH terms for PubMed/Embase ("draft, then librarian-verify" is the professional standard — medical librarians report AI-drafted strings are strong starting points and poor final ones).
  • 3. Screening: Elicit and systematic-review platforms with AI assistance triage titles/abstracts against your inclusion criteria. Governance rule from the Cochrane world: AI may assist screening, but human adjudication of borderline calls — and documentation of the AI’s role — is required for a defensible methods section.
  • 4. Extraction: structured tables (population, n, intervention, outcomes, effect sizes, risk-of-bias notes) generated per paper, then spot-audited: verify a random 20% by hand and report your audit in methods. Auditable acceleration is publishable; unaudited acceleration is not.
  • 5. Synthesis: ask for contradictions, not just summaries: "Where do these studies disagree, and what design differences could explain it?" — the question that turns a literature pile into a discussion section.
  • 6. Writing: outline → section drafts → your intellectual pass (the argument must be yours) → AI polish pass for clarity and concision → reference verification, one by one, by opening them. The fabricated-citation retractions now on record all share one feature: nobody opened the references.

Statistics: the guardrails

  • Legitimate: "Which test fits this design and why? What assumptions must I check? Interpret this output in plain language. What would invalidate this conclusion?" AI as statistics tutor and interpretation checker is transformative for clinician-researchers.
  • Illegitimate: letting AI choose and run analyses you don’t understand, or generate results you can’t defend at a podium. The test: if a reviewer asks "why this test?", the answer must be yours.
  • The p-hacking amplifier: AI makes running twenty analyses trivially easy — which makes pre-registration and stated primary outcomes MORE important, not less. Speed without discipline manufactures false findings faster.

Integrity: what journals and institutions now require

  • Authorship: ICMJE-aligned journals prohibit listing AI as an author — authorship requires accountability, which machines cannot bear.
  • Disclosure: most major journals require describing AI use in methods or acknowledgments (which tool, for what tasks). Norms vary — check the specific journal, every submission.
  • Peer review: many funders and journals prohibit feeding confidential manuscripts into AI tools for review purposes — confidentiality of submission survives the AI era intact.
  • Data: research data carries its own consent and governance terms; "de-identified for care" is not automatically "approved for AI processing" — check your protocol and IRB/ethics terms.
🧪 Interactive Lab

Act as a methodologist and co-investigator. My research interest: [describe loosely]. (1) Refine it into three PICO-format questions ranked by feasibility for a clinician with limited time and no funding. (2) For the best one: draft a PubMed Boolean search string with MeSH terms, an inclusion/exclusion table, and a data-extraction template. (3) List the statistical approach with its assumptions, and every point where I must involve a librarian, statistician, or ethics committee. (4) Draft my AI-use disclosure statement for a journal.

plAIbox™ (graded): the mini-review. One focused question, ten papers, AI-assisted screening and extraction with a documented 20% hand-audit, a 500-word synthesis whose every citation you opened, and a methods-style AI-disclosure paragraph. Two weeks; mentor plays peer reviewer. Past students have expanded this artifact into published letters and posters.

quiz.q: PICO stands for…
quiz.x: PICO forces answerable structure onto vague interests — the highest-leverage ten minutes in research.

quiz.q: The professional standard for AI-drafted search strings is…
opts: Draft with AI, verify with a medical librarian
quiz.x: AI strings are strong starts and poor finals; librarian verification is the quality gate.

quiz.q: Defensible AI-assisted screening requires…
opts: Human adjudication of borderline calls plus documentation of AI’s role
quiz.x: Methods sections must describe the AI’s role; humans own inclusion decisions.

quiz.q: The extraction-audit rule taught here is…
opts: Hand-verify a random ~20% and report the audit
quiz.x: Auditable acceleration is publishable; unaudited extraction is a validity hole reviewers will find.

quiz.q: The synthesis question that generates discussion sections is…
opts: Where do studies disagree and what design differences explain it
quiz.x: Contradiction-hunting converts summary into scholarship.

quiz.q: Fabricated-citation scandals share the common failure that…
quiz.x: Opening every reference is the cheap, absolute defense.

quiz.q: AI as statistics helper is legitimate for…
opts: Choosing and running analyses you don’t understand
Test-selection tutoring, assumption checks, and interpretation you can defend
quiz.x: The podium test: the ‘why this test’ answer must be yours.

quiz.q: AI increases p-hacking risk because…
opts: Running many analyses becomes trivially easy, so pre-registration matters more

modules.t: AI for Medical Students: Study Systems
modules.d: Boards, wards, and OSCEs: building the study machine that compounds — with the science of why it works.
modules.body:
The learning science first — why these systems work

Two findings dominate a century of learning research: active recall (testing yourself beats re-reading by large margins) and spaced repetition (reviews timed just before forgetting lock in retention). Medical students discovered this at scale — spaced-repetition flashcards became boards-prep orthodoxy — but making good cards and good practice questions was always the bottleneck. AI removes the bottleneck. What follows is the study machine, component by component.

Component 1: The card factory (active recall at scale)

  • "From these lecture notes, generate cloze-deletion flashcards: one fact per card, no card answerable without the concept, include a one-line ‘why it matters clinically’ on the back. Output in a format I can import to Anki."
  • Quality control is yours: delete cards testing trivia, keep cards testing decisions. A 40-card deck you curated beats a 400-card dump.

Component 2: The question generator (boards-grade practice)

  • "Write 5 USMLE-style clinical vignettes on [topic]: two-step reasoning (finding → mechanism → answer), plausible distractors representing real student errors, and explanations for why EVERY option is right or wrong."
  • The explanation-for-every-option requirement is the pedagogy: wrong-answer autopsy is where discrimination skill is built.
  • Calibration warning: AI-generated questions are excellent practice and imperfect calibrators — difficulty drifts from real exams. Use question banks for calibration; use AI for volume, weak-spot targeting, and explanation depth.

Component 3: The standardized patient (voice mode changes everything)

  • "You are a standardized patient: 54-year-old with an undisclosed diagnosis (choose one appropriate to chest pain teaching). Present realistically; volunteer nothing; reveal only what I elicit. After 8 minutes, break character and score my history-taking: organization, red-flag coverage, empathy, and the three questions I failed to ask."
  • Run it by voice. Students consistently report the first session is startling — the hesitation, the missed questions, the timing all feel real. Repeat weekly with rotating chief complaints.

Component 4: OSCE & communication rehearsal

  • Counseling stations: smoking cessation, new-diagnosis diabetes, inhaler technique — request a rubric-scored debrief after each.
  • Breaking bad news with SPIKES (Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Empathy, Strategy): "Play the patient’s spouse; I will deliver difficult news; score my SPIKES adherence step by step and quote the exact sentences that landed well or poorly." Rehearsing the hardest conversations in a consequence-free room is a gift no previous generation of students had.

Component 5: The concept rescuer

  • The three-level ladder: "Explain [renal tubular acidosis] to a 12-year-old, then to a nursing student, then to an attending — same core truth, three altitudes." When you can follow all three, you own the concept.
  • The Feynman inversion: "I will explain [concept] to YOU; interrupt at every gap or error." Teaching the machine exposes what re-reading conceals.

The integrity line for students

  • AI on graded work follows your school’s policy, full stop — and disclosure norms from Module 5 apply to student research identically.
  • The deeper point: shortcuts on formation become gaps at the bedside. Use AI to practice MORE, never to practice less. The machine is your sparring partner, not your substitute.
🧪 Interactive Lab — your first simulated patient

You are a standardized patient for a medical student. Choose an undisclosed diagnosis appropriate for teaching [chief complaint of my choice]. Present realistically with a natural personality; volunteer nothing; reveal findings only when properly elicited. After 8 minutes (or when I say STOP), break character and give me: a score out of 10 for organization, red-flag coverage, and empathy; the three most important questions I failed to ask; and the diagnosis with the discriminating features I found or missed.

plAIbox™ (graded): build and run your study OS for one full week — card factory, question generator, one voice-mode patient, one OSCE rehearsal — and report: hours spent vs your previous baseline, question-bank score movement, and the single component you will keep forever. Mentors review the system design, not just the report.

modules.d: Devices, not chatbots: reading validation studies, questioning vendors, and the global-health frontier.
modules.body:
A different species of AI

Everything so far has been assistive text. This module is about regulated medical devices: algorithms cleared by the FDA and international counterparts, with defined intended uses, validation dossiers, and post-market obligations. Hundreds of such clearances now exist — roughly three-quarters in radiology — and the number compounds yearly. A clinician who can read a validation claim is worth ten who can repeat a headline.

Where cleared AI actually works today

  • Radiology triage: intracranial hemorrhage, pulmonary embolism, and pneumothorax flags that re-order the reading worklist — minutes saved on true emergencies, with the radiologist still reading everything.
  • Stroke coordination: platforms that detect large-vessel occlusion on CT angiography and alert the intervention team directly — among the best-evidenced time-to-treatment improvements in deployed clinical AI.
  • Mammography: AI-supported screening validated in large prospective European programs — maintained or improved detection with substantially reduced radiologist workload.
  • Ophthalmology: autonomous diabetic-retinopathy screening at point of care — historic as the first autonomous AI diagnostic clearance, extending screening to clinics with no ophthalmologist.
  • Cardiology: ECG algorithms flagging low-EF and arrhythmia risk from routine tracings; smartwatch AF detection pushing rhythm screening into daily life (with a real conversation to have about false positives in low-risk populations).
  • Pathology: cleared digital-pathology assistants for prostate biopsy review and mitosis counting — the microscope’s turn.

How to read a validation claim (the core skill)

  • Population: validated on whom? Age, ethnicity, scanner types, disease prevalence. Performance does not travel automatically — the distribution-shift lesson from Module 1, now with regulatory stakes.
  • Metrics at YOUR prevalence: sensitivity/specificity are prevalence-independent, but positive predictive value collapses in low-prevalence settings. A 95%-sensitive, 90%-specific tool screening a 1%-prevalence population generates ~10 false alarms per true case. Do this arithmetic before every deployment conversation.
  • Ground truth: against what standard was it measured — expert consensus, biopsy, outcomes? Weak ground truth inflates claims.
  • Prospective vs retrospective: retrospective excellence routinely shrinks in prospective deployment; ask which one the claim rests on.

The five vendor questions (bring these to every demo)

  • 1. What is your validation population, and how does it differ from mine?
  • 2. Sensitivity, specificity — and PPV at MY prevalence?
  • 3. How does it integrate into workflow, and what happens when it is down?
  • 4. Who bears liability for algorithm-influenced misses, and what does my insurer say?
  • 5. What is the post-deployment monitoring plan for drift, and who watches it?

The global-health frontier

The most consequential deployments may be where specialists are scarcest: WHO now conditionally recommends computer-aided detection for TB screening on chest radiographs in settings without radiologists; retinopathy screening runs in primary-care clinics; AI-guided ultrasound lets minimally trained operators acquire diagnostic-quality cardiac and obstetric images. Evaluate these with the same five questions PLUS the field realities: connectivity, power, maintenance, and local validation — a tool validated in London serving Lagos deserves Lagos validation.

Patients arrive pre-briefed

Your patients consult chatbots before consulting you. The productive script: acknowledge ("good that you’re researching"), correct specifically (not "don’t Google" but "here’s what that source missed about your case"), and redirect to sources you trust. The clinician who engages the AI-informed patient keeps the relationship; the one who scoffs loses it.

🧪 Interactive Lab — the PPV reality check

Act as a biostatistics tutor. Walk me through positive and negative predictive value step by step for a screening AI with sensitivity [95]% and specificity [90]% at disease prevalences of 1%, 5%, and 20%. Show the 2x2 tables, the false-alarms-per-true-case ratio at each prevalence, and then explain in two paragraphs — suitable for a department meeting — why an impressive tool can still flood a low-prevalence clinic with false positives, and what deployment choices mitigate it.

modules.t: Capstone: Your Clinical AI Workflow & Governance Note
modules.d: Two weeks of measured deployment, a policy your department could adopt, and the presentation that proves it.
modules.body:
What this capstone is — and is not

This is not an essay. It is a deployment: one AI-augmented workflow running in your real professional life for two measured weeks, wrapped in the governance thinking that would let your department adopt it tomorrow. Graduates have used this exact artifact to become their institution’s AI lead, to win pilot funding, and — in one memorable case — to talk a hospital out of a bad vendor contract.

Component 1 — The workflow (choose one, go deep)

  • Documentation: a scribe or structured-note pipeline (Modules 2–3) across ≥20 encounters.
  • Patient education: a literacy-tiered, bilingual instruction system for your three commonest discharge scenarios.
  • Study OS: the full Module 6 machine, run for two weeks with score data (students).
  • Research pipeline: the Module 5 mini-review executed end to end.
  • Evidence workflow: a foreground-question routine using the Module 4 stack, logged across two weeks of real questions.

Component 2 — The measurement (numbers, honestly)

  • Time: baseline vs deployed, measured not estimated (note-completion minutes, questions-answered-per-hour, cards-per-lecture — whatever fits your workflow).
  • Quality: a defined check (edits per note, verification failures caught, score movement, mentor-rated samples).
  • The error log: your five most instructive AI failures from the fortnight, categorized (factual / inferential / omission / tone), each with how you caught it. Examiners read this section first — it is where judgment shows.

Component 3 — The governance note (one page, adoptable)

  • Data rules: which data classes may enter which tools (your Module 2 green/amber/red paths, made local).
  • Approved tools & verification standard: named tools, the 60-second rule operationalized, citation-opening policy.
  • Disclosure: to patients (scribes/consent), in documentation, in academic work.
  • Review cadence: who re-examines this policy, how often, and what triggers early review (new tool, incident, guideline change). Model it on WHO’s six principles — autonomy, safety, transparency, accountability, equity, sustainability — and say so; reviewers upstream of you will recognize the scaffold.

Component 4 — The tool matrix

Your Modules 3–4 selection matrices completed with CURRENT verified pricing and terms for your context — the perishable homework that proves you can re-do it whenever the market moves.

Component 5 — The presentation

Ten minutes to the mentor panel, structured as if to your department: the problem, the workflow, the numbers, the failures and catches, the governance ask. Then ten minutes of adversarial questions — expect the PPV arithmetic, the liability question, and "what breaks first at scale?"

Grading rubric: deployment reality (30%) · measurement honesty (25%) · error-log insight (20%) · governance adoptability (15%) · presentation under fire (10%). Pass mark 70%. Distinction earns the right to mentor next cohort’s medical track.
Certification: completing all module quizzes (≥70% each) and the capstone earns the AI Unlocked: Medicine certificate, printable from your Certificates tab, signed by Innocent Forteh, Program Manager. Continue with AI in Public Health for population-scale applications, or Level 2: OPERATE to automate what you built here.
